title: The particular judgment (CCC 1021–1022)
hookLine: at death each person meets Christ

cards: Three crosses on a hill outside Jerusalem. On one side of Jesus, a criminal mocks him. On the other, a second criminal tells the first to stop: we deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong.
Then he asks one thing: remember me when you come into your kingdom. He has no time left to make amends, no time to prove he's changed. And the answer he gets doesn't say later, or someday.
It says today. That one word is where the Catechism starts on what happens at the moment of death.

teach.h: THIS DAY THOU SHALT BE WITH ME.
teach.b: This path heard the short version on day three hundred twenty-five: each person is judged by love. From the cross, in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise."

The Catechism points to that line, and to Jesus's story of the rich man and Lazarus, to teach what Catholics call the particular judgment. Particular, because it's personal: one person, one life, at the moment it ends.

teach.h: ONCE TO DIE, AND AFTER THIS.
teach.b: The Letter to the Hebrews says it plainly: "it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment." At death, the Catechism teaches, each person meets Christ, and their whole life is seen in his light.

The Catechism names three ways: into heaven at once; into heaven through a purification first, which Catholics call purgatory; or, for someone who has finally refused God's love, lasting separation from him.
It doesn't say who goes where. Third, the measure.
The Catechism borrows a line from Saint John of the Cross: in the evening of life, we will be judged on love. Not on titles, not on how impressive a life looked. Fourth, the hope.

Saint Paul wrote that now we see only dimly, as in a dark mirror, "but then face to face." Judgment, for Catholics, isn't a file read out by a stranger. It's meeting someone, and seeing yourself the way he sees you.
The thief on the cross had no record to show. He had one honest request, and a face turned toward Christ.

how: Catholics pray for a holy death and for the dead, and some end the day with an examination of conscience, looking back over the day before God.

games.q: you're the second criminal, dying beside Jesus. you have minutes, and nothing to show for your life. what do you say?
o: join the other man and mock him

practice: Some Catholics end the day with a short look back called an examen; this is a small version. Walk back through today slowly, like watching a film, and ask where there was love, given, received or missed.
If you pray, imagine looking at the day alongside Christ; if you don't, look at it the way the kindest person you know would.

wordCard.voice: The particular judgment. Catholics believe that at death each person meets Christ, and their life is seen in his light, judged, as John of the Cross put it, on love. Today's word.
